claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an as-reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Ab initio calculations are too time-consuming for high-throughput alloy-structure prediction.
CALPHAD screening can require significant computational resources and can be limited by the lack of reliable HEA databases.
Existing HEA property-prediction studies focus primarily on yield strength or hardness rather than toughness.
Generic machine-learning approaches are less precise for toughness and for hierarchical-microstructure effects.
A physics-informed machine-learned interatomic potential can be calibrated with a minimal dataset to capture HfNbTiVAl10's hierarchical microstructure and multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Explicitly encoding local chemical heterogeneity and mesoscale features will reproduce stress redistribution and local deformation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Descriptors based on local bond stiffness, misfit volumes, and chemical fluctuations, combined with machine learning, will reproduce the alloy's deformation and fracture mechanisms.
Interatomic-potential simulations can agree quantitatively with first-principles calculations and experiments for relevant structural and elastic properties.
The proposed potential will predict Young's modulus within 10% of experiment.
The proposed potential will predict yield strength within 10% of experiment.
The proposed potential will predict fracture toughness within 10% of experiment.
The proposed approach will be approximately ten times faster than conventional first-principles, CALPHAD, or brute-force machine-learning approaches.
The model will remain reliable under room-temperature uniaxial tensile and mode-I fracture loading if the calibrated hierarchical microstructure is preserved.
The model will lose reliability if processing causes phase decomposition or unexpected second-phase formation.
The model will lose reliability at defect concentrations not represented in its training data.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts about a ten-fold speedup, but the benchmark falsifies it only below a five-fold speedup. A result between 5× and 10× would miss the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
The outcome claim applies a 10% bound to each property, whereas the falsification rule refers to an average deviation. Averaging could conceal a greater-than-10% error for an individual property.
